quick: Hyperphosphatemia (dialysis): start 2 tablets (1 g ferric iron) 3 times daily with meals; IDA in non-dialysis CKD: start 1 tablet 3 times daily with food
Take with meals (phosphate binding) or with food (iron deficiency indication)
May cause excess iron; use only if clearly needed and monitor iron parameters
Iron is present in milk; generally considered compatible with monitoring
Indicated specifically in chronic kidney disease (dialysis and non-dialysis)
Not studied; caution in conditions of iron overload
Serum phosphorus, iron studies (ferritin, TSAT), hemoglobin; avoid iron overload
summary: Ferric citrate is an iron-based oral agent with two distinct approved uses: as a phosphate binder to control serum phosphorus in adults with chronic kidney disease on dialysis, and as an iron-replacement product to treat iron deficiency anemia in adults with chronic kidney disease not on dialysis. Taken with meals, the ferric iron binds dietary phosphate in the gut to form insoluble ferric phosphate that is excreted in feces; some iron is also absorbed, which can raise iron stores. The main risks are iron accumulation (avoid in iron overload) and gastrointestinal effects, especially discolored (dark/black) stools.
indications: Control of serum phosphorus levels in adults with chronic kidney disease on dialysis
Treatment of iron deficiency anemia in adults with chronic kidney disease not on dialysis

dosage.d: Start 2 tablets (each 1 g ferric citrate = 210 mg ferric iron) three times daily with meals
dosage.n: Titrate by 1-2 tablets/day to target serum phosphorus; average ~8 tablets/day, max about 12 tablets/day

dosage.c: Iron deficiency anemia in non-dialysis CKD
dosage.d: Start 1 tablet (210 mg ferric iron) three times daily with food
dosage.n: Titrate as needed; max about 12 tablets/day

admin: Take tablets with meals (for phosphate control) or with food (for iron deficiency anemia)
Swallow tablets whole; titrate the dose based on serum phosphorus or iron/hemoglobin response
Separate from oral medications whose absorption may be affected (e.g., doxycycline 1 hour before; ciprofloxacin 2 hours before or after)
Expect harmless dark or black discoloration of the stool
moa: Ferric citrate provides ferric iron that, in the gastrointestinal tract, binds dietary phosphate to form insoluble ferric phosphate, which is excreted in the feces; this lowers phosphate absorption and serum phosphorus in patients with chronic kidney disease. Additionally, some ferric iron is solubilized and absorbed across the gut, increasing iron stores and supporting erythropoiesis, which underlies its use in iron deficiency anemia.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to ferric citrate or any component
relative: Conditions with increased iron stores or repeated blood transfusions
Active or symptomatic gastrointestinal disease (gastritis, ulcers, inflammatory bowel disease)
Concomitant oral medications with iron-sensitive absorption
monitor: Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation (avoid iron overload)

preg: Ferric citrate increases iron absorption and can lead to excess iron; overdose of iron is dangerous in pregnancy. Use only if clearly needed, monitor maternal iron parameters, and avoid iron accumulation. Untreated hyperphosphatemia or anemia also pose risks.
lact: Iron is present in human milk. Ferric citrate is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding when used as indicated, but maternal iron status should be monitored to avoid overload.
renal: Ferric citrate is specifically indicated in patients with chronic kidney disease, both dialysis-dependent (phosphate binding) and non-dialysis (iron deficiency anemia). No additional renal dose adjustment beyond the indication-specific titration is required.
hepatic: Ferric citrate has not been specifically studied in hepatic impairment. Use with caution in conditions associated with iron overload, which can affect the liver.

major: Oral drugs that chelate or bind iron with narrow margins (e.g., certain antibiotics) - reduced absorption
moderate: Doxycycline - take at least 1 hour before ferric citrate
Ciprofloxacin - take at least 2 hours before or after ferric citrate
Other oral iron-sensitive drugs (levothyroxine, bisphosphonates, mycophenolate, some fluoroquinolones/tetracyclines) - separate dosing
minor: Antacids/agents altering gastric pH (may affect iron solubility)
interactions.food: Take with meals (phosphate binding) or with food (iron deficiency); food is needed for the binding effect
interactions.diagnostics: Raises serum ferritin and transferrin saturation; stool may test falsely positive for occult blood is not typical, but stool is discolored dark/black

serious: Accidental iron overdose, especially in children (can be fatal)
emergency: Accidental overdose in a child (medical emergency - iron poisoning)

monitoring: Iron parameters: serum ferritin and transferrin saturation (avoid overload)
counsel: Take with meals or food as directed - it works by binding phosphate in your food or by replacing iron
Your bowel movements may turn dark or black, which is harmless
Keep tablets out of the reach of children - accidental iron overdose can be fatal to a child
Tell your doctor about all other medicines; some need to be taken at a different time
Do not take other iron supplements unless your doctor approves
Report ongoing diarrhea, constipation, or stomach pain
pk: Phosphate-lowering effect develops over days to weeks of regular dosing
Acts locally in the gut; iron absorption increases serum iron indices over time
Not applicable in the conventional sense; ferric phosphate is excreted in feces
Effect maintained with consistent dosing at every meal
Store at room temperature in the original container; protect from moisture; keep desiccant in the bottle
pearls: Dual-purpose iron-based drug: phosphate binder in dialysis CKD and iron repletion in non-dialysis CKD
Unlike non-iron binders, it both lowers phosphate AND raises iron stores - can reduce the need for IV iron and ESAs in dialysis patients
Monitor ferritin and transferrin saturation to avoid iron overload; contraindicated in hemochromatosis
Counsel patients that dark/black stools are expected and benign, not gastrointestinal bleeding
Keep away from children - a single mismanaged iron-containing product overdose can be lethal in young children
missed: If a dose is missed, skip it and take the next dose with the next meal at the usual time; do not double the dose. Because ferric citrate must be taken with food to bind phosphate, do not take a missed dose between meals on an empty stomach.
overdose: Iron overdose, particularly in children, can be serious or fatal. Excessive iron causes gastrointestinal corrosion (vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea), then metabolic acidosis, shock, hepatotoxicity, and coagulopathy. Management includes supportive care, assessment of serum iron, whole-bowel irrigation in significant ingestions, and chelation with deferoxamine for severe systemic iron toxicity. Seek emergency care immediately for suspected overdose.
